citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-noise Gaussian sequence model with $\sigma>0$, a fixed complete positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ for an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator $T:X\to Y$, and a truth with coordinates $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ in $\ell^2$. Write $\lambda_j=s_j^2$ and let $\xi_j$ be the independent standard-normal noise coordinates. Let $q_\alpha$ be nonnegative and satisfy $0\le\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$, $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$, and $q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\le q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)$ whenever $m_1<m_2$. For each candidate $m$, form the finite sums
$$
X_{m,N}:=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j\bigr)v_j.
$$
The conclusion below includes the existence of their limit $\widehat x_m$ in $L^2(\Omega;X)$. Put $f_m:=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $B_m:=\|f_m-x\|_X$, and $v_m:=\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-f_m\|_X^2$. Then $\widehat x_m$ is a measurable $X$-valued random element with finite second moment and
$$
\mathbb E\|\widehat x_m-x\|_X^2=B_m^2+v_m,\qquad v_m=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
If $m_1<m_2$, then $B_{m_2}\le B_{m_1}$, $\|f_{m_2}-f_{m_1}\|_X\le B_{m_1}$, and
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\mathbb E\| (\widehat x_{m_2}-f_{m_2})-(\widehat x_{m_1}-f_{m_1})\|_X^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2\le v_{m_2}.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces, let $S=T^*T$, and let $(s_j,v_j,u_j)$ be a fixed positive singular system with $\lambda_j=s_j^2$. Let $Z$ be a real isonormal Gaussian process on $Y$, meaning that $g\mapsto Z(g)$ is linear into $L^2$, is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. In the weak observation experiment $Y_x(g)=\langle Tx,g\rangle_Y+\sigma Z(g)$ with known noise standard deviation $\sigma>0$, use the ordered filter $q_\alpha$, the geometric-variance candidates $\alpha_0>\cdots>\alpha_{m_{\max}}$, and variances $v_m=\sigma^2\sum_j\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2$ from the preceding definition. For each candidate index $m$, the regularized estimator $\widehat x_m$ is the $L^2$ limit of its finite singular-coordinate sums; its $j$th coordinate is $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\theta_j+\sigma s_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\xi_j$, where $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$ and $\xi_j=Z(u_j)$.

For $0\le m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, set
$$
v_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_j\bigl(q_{\alpha_{m_2}}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_{m_1}}(\lambda_j)\bigr)^2
$$
and let $N_{m_1,m_2}$ be the norm of the centered estimator difference divided by $\sigma$. For $x>0$, define its upper quantile by
$$
z_{m_1,m_2}(x):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N_{m_1,m_2}>z)\le e^{-x}\}.
$$
Given fixed $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$, put $x_m:=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)$ and $\eta_{m_1,m_2}:=\sigma z_{m_1,m_2}(x_{m_1})+\beta\sqrt{v_{m_1,m_2}}$. Accept an index $m_1$ exactly when $\|\widehat x_{m_1}-\widehat x_{m_2}\|_X\le\eta_{m_1,m_2}$ for every $m_2$ with $m_1<m_2\le m_{\max}$, and output the smallest accepted index $\widehat m$ and parameter $\widehat\alpha=\alpha_{\widehat m}$. The condition for $m_1=m_{\max}$ is vacuous, so the finite search always returns an index. This rule uses only the observed sequence, the known operator and filter, the noise level, the fixed candidate grid, and $\beta,\gamma$; it does not use $x$ or its source index $\varphi$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(\xi_j)_{j\ge1}$ be given real random variables on a probability space such that every finite subfamily is independent and each variable has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$. Let $a_j\ge0$ be deterministic with $v:=\sum_j a_j<\infty$, and put $u:=\sup_j a_j$ and $w:=\sum_j a_j^2$. The nonnegative series $Q:=\sum_j a_j\xi_j^2$ is finite almost surely. Define $N:=\sqrt Q$ on that event and set $N=0$ on its null complement. Then
$$\mathbb E N^2=v,\qquad \mathbb E N^4=v^2+2w\le3v^2.$$
For every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P\{N^2>v+2\sqrt{wt}+2ut\}\le e^{-t},\qquad \mathbb P\{N>\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}\}\le e^{-t}.$$
The upper quantile $q(t):=\inf\{z\ge0:\mathbb P(N>z)\le e^{-t}\}$ is finite and satisfies
$$\mathbb P(N>q(t))\le e^{-t},\qquad q(t)\le\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}.$$
These conclusions include $v=0$, in which case $N=q(t)=0$ almost surely. For a Gaussian series in a fixed orthonormal coordinate system with coordinate variances $a_j$, $N$ is its norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T:X\to Y$ be an injective compact linear operator of infinite rank between separable real Hilbert spaces (each with a countable dense subset), and assume $T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, meaning that for its positive singular values $s_j$ the sum $\sum_{j\ge1}s_j^2$ is finite. Put $S=T^*T$, $\lambda_j=s_j^2$, and $\lambda_1=\|S\|$, with the positive eigenvalues listed with multiplicity in nonincreasing order. Let $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and strictly increasing with $\varphi(0)=0$, and take its inverse on its range. Assume the paper's convexity condition on the spectral range: $x\mapsto x\varphi^{-1}(\sqrt{x})$ is convex for $0\le x\le\varphi(\lambda_1)^2$. Define the source class $\mathcal W_\varphi(\rho):=\{\varphi(S)w:w\in X,\ \|w\|_X\le\rho\}$ for $\rho>0$; equivalently, it is the source ball with singular-value index $\psi(t)=\varphi(t^2)$.

An ordered spectral filter is a family of functions $q_\alpha:[0,\lambda_1]\to[0,\infty)$ indexed by a set $\mathcal A\subset(0,\infty)$ with $0$ as an accumulation point, such that for constants $C_q'<\infty$ and $C_q''=1$,
$$
0\le\alpha q_\alpha(x)\le C_q',\qquad 0\le xq_\alpha(x)\le1,
$$
and $q_\alpha(x)\le q_{\widetilde\alpha}(x)$ whenever $\widetilde\alpha<\alpha$, for every $x\in[0,\lambda_1]$. The index function $\varphi$ is a qualification of this filter if for some $C_\varphi<\infty$,
$$
\sup_{0\le x\le\lambda_1}\varphi(x)(1-xq_\alpha(x))\le C_\varphi\varphi(\alpha)\qquad(\alpha\in\mathcal A).
$$

For $\alpha\in\mathcal A$, define the variance function
$$
V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2.
$$
For $\sigma>0$, a decreasing candidate sequence $(\alpha_m)_{m\in\mathbb N_0}$ in $\mathcal A$ has **geometric variance growth** if $V_{T,q}(\alpha_0)>0$ and there are constants $1<\theta_1\le\theta_2<\infty$ such that
$$
\theta_1\le\frac{V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)}{V_{T,q}(\alpha_{m-1})}\le\theta_2\qquad(m\ge1).
$$
Set $v_m:=\sigma^2V_{T,q}(\alpha_m)$ and
$$
u_m:=\sigma^2\sup_{j\ge1}\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)^2,
$$
the operator norm of the estimator-noise covariance in the singular basis. The bound $q_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le C_q'/\alpha_m$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j<\infty$ make each $u_m$ and $v_m$ finite. The finite candidate set ends at
$$
m_{\max}:=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:v_m\ge1\}.
$$
The geometric lower bound $v_m\ge v_0\theta_1^m$ makes this index finite.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact and bounded. Put $S=A^*A$. By
[[lem-compact-gram-operator-is-positive-and-has-kernel]], $S$ is compact,
positive, and self-adjoint, with $\ker S=\ker A$. Let $\Sigma$ be the set of
nonzero eigenvalues of $S$ and $P_t$ the orthogonal projection onto the
eigenspace of $t\in\Sigma$; let $P_0$ be the orthogonal projection onto
$\ker S$. The compact spectral multiplier of a bounded scalar function
$q:\{0\}\cup\Sigma\to\mathbb F$ is
$$q(S)x:=q(0)P_0x+\sum_{t\in\Sigma}q(t)P_tx,$$
where the finite-subset net converges in norm by
[[lem-compact-spectral-multiplier-is-well-defined]]. For $\nu>0$, define
$S^\nu$ by the multiplier $q_\nu(0)=0$ and $q_\nu(t)=t^\nu$ for $t>0$.
This multiplier is bounded: if $t\in\Sigma$ and $u\in E_t$ is a unit vector,
then $0<t=\|Su\|\le\|S\|$, so $|q_\nu(t)|\le\|S\|^\nu$.

For $\lambda>0$, the Tikhonov filter and residual filter are
$$g_\lambda(t)=\frac1{t+\lambda},\qquad r_\lambda(t)=1-tg_\lambda(t)=\frac{\lambda}{t+\lambda}.$$
The Tikhonov solution for data $y_\delta\in Y$ is
$$x_\lambda^\delta=g_\lambda(S)A^*y_\delta =(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*y_\delta.$$
Indeed, the spectral decomposition gives $S+\lambda I_X$ the multiplier
$t+\lambda$ on each $E_t$ and $\lambda$ on $\ker S$, so $g_\lambda(S)$ is
its inverse, whose existence is also supplied by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]].
The source condition of order $\nu>0$ and radius $R\ge0$ means that
$x^\dagger=S^\nu w$ for some $w\in X$ with $\|w\|\le R$. A family of
filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has
qualification at least $p>0$ when, for each $0<\nu\le p$, some finite
constant $C_\nu\ge0$ satisfies
$$t^\nu|r_\alpha(t)|\le C_\nu\alpha^\nu \quad\text{for every }\alpha>0\text{ and }t\in\Sigma.$$
When $\Sigma=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Work in the supplied singular coordinates, and write $f_m=\mathbb E\widehat x_m$, $\varepsilon_m=\widehat x_m-f_m$, and $b_{a,b}=\|f_b-f_a\|_X$. By [F1] all these variables have finite second moments and $R_m=b_m^2+v_m$. The finite comparison conditions are measurable, and [F2] ensures an accepted index exists. Thus $\widehat m$ is a measurable finite-valued index. Fix $k=m_*$; its defining condition gives $b_{a,b}\le\beta\sqrt{v_{a,b}}$ whenever $k\le a<b\le M$.

For later use, qualification gives $b_m^2\le\rho^2C_\varphi^2\varphi(\alpha_m)^2$. The filter bounds give $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)^2\le C_q'/\alpha$ and $\lambda q_\alpha(\lambda)^2\le(C_q')^2\lambda/\alpha^2$. With $C=\max\{C_q',(C_q')^2\}$, splitting eigenvalues at $\alpha$ and summing nonnegative terms therefore gives $$V_{T,q}(\alpha):=\sum_j\lambda_jq_\alpha(\lambda_j)^2\le\frac C{\alpha^2}\left(\alpha\Sigma(\alpha)+\sum_{\lambda_j<\alpha}\lambda_j\right)=\frac C{\alpha^2}\int_0^\alpha\Sigma(t)\,dt\le CC_SS(\alpha)/\alpha.$$ The equality follows by integrating each indicator $1_{\{t\le\lambda_j\}}$; [F5] justifies the interchange. Further $u_m\le C_q'\sigma^2/\alpha_m$, since $\lambda_jq_{\alpha_m}(\lambda_j)\le1$.

The centered difference $G_{a,b}$ has coordinate variances $\sigma^2\lambda_j(q_{\alpha_b}(\lambda_j)-q_{\alpha_a}(\lambda_j))^2$. By nonnegative coordinate ordering their sum and supremum satisfy $v_{a,b}\le v_b$ and $u_{a,b}\le u_b$. Applying [F3] to their squared weights gives $$\sigma z_{a,b}(t)\le\sqrt{v_{a,b}}+\sqrt{2u_{a,b}t},\qquad \mathbb E\|\varepsilon_m\|^4\le3v_m^2.$$ Also the probability of exceeding the actual pairwise quantile is at most $e^{-t}$, including a degenerate difference. These are statements about the supplied normal sequence; no new infinite product law or general Gaussian concentration theorem is needed.

For the rates let $s=\sigma^2\downarrow0$ and $L=\log(1/s)$. The initial variance is $v_0=sV_{T,q}(\alpha_0)$ with a fixed positive factor, and the geometric lower ratio implies $M\le1+\log(1/v_0)/\log	heta_1=O(L)$. In the mild case put $D=2
u+1+1/a$, $t=s^{1/D}L^{2	au/D}$ and $r=s^{2
u/D}L^{-2	au(1+1/a)/D}$. In the severe case put $p=1/\vartheta\ge2$, $D=2
u+1$, $t=s^{1/D}L^{(2	au+p)/D}$ and $r=s^{2
u/D}L^{(2
u p-2	au)/D}$. In either case $\log(1/t)\asymp L$, $r	o0$, $r/s	o\infty$, and direct substitution gives $\varphi(t)^2\asymp sS(t)/t\asymp r$. All implicit constants in the rest of the argument are independent of the truth in the fixed source ball and of sufficiently small $s$.

On $\{\widehat m\le k\}$, acceptance gives $\|\widehat x_{\widehat m}-\widehat x_k\|\le\eta_{\widehat m,k}$ when $\widehat m<k$, and the difference is zero when equality holds. For $m<k$, $x_m=2(1+\gamma)\log(v_{m+1}/v_0)\le2(1+\gamma)\log(v_k/v_0)$, so step 2.1 bounds every $\eta_{m,k}$ by $D_k$. The triangle inequality in mean square consequently bounds the early-selection contribution by $(\sqrt{R_k}+D_k)^2$. For $k=0$, this uses the identically zero difference and hence $D_0=0$.

For $m>k$, the event $\{\widehat m=m\}$ implies rejection of $m-1$. Its oracle bias bound from step 1.1 shows that a rejecting comparison with $\ell\ge m$ must satisfy $\|G_{m-1,\ell}\|>\sigma z_{m-1,\ell}(x_{m-1})$. The union bound over $M-m+1$ such comparisons and the quantile-tail property from step 2.1 therefore give $\mathbb P(\widehat m=m)\le p_m$. Similarly $\{\widehat m>k\}$ implies rejection of $k$, so $\mathbb P(\widehat m>k)\le P_k$. Here $e^{-x_{m-1}}=(v_0/v_m)^{2(1+\gamma)}$ exactly.

Let $j$ be the first candidate with $v_j\ge r$. For small $s$, $v_0<r<1$, so this index exists and $r\le v_j\le\theta_2r$. Step 1.2 implies $r\le CsS(\alpha_j)/\alpha_j$. First $\alpha_j\to0$: otherwise a subsequence bounded away from zero has bounded $S(\alpha_j)/\alpha_j$, contradicting $r/s\to\infty$. In the mild case the function $S(\alpha)/\alpha$ is comparable to $\alpha^{-1-1/a}$, so the last inequality and $r\asymp st^{-1-1/a}$ give $\alpha_j\le C't$. In the severe case it is comparable to $h(\alpha)=\alpha^{-1}(\log(1/\alpha))^p$. For any fixed $A>1$, $h(At)/h(t)\to1/A$ as $t\downarrow0$; since $h$ is decreasing for small positive arguments, choosing $A$ larger than the fixed comparison constant gives the same conclusion $\alpha_j\le C't$. Qualification and $\varphi(C't)^2\asymp\varphi(t)^2$ now give $b_j^2\le C''r$.

Cauchy–Schwarz and step 2.1 give $\mathbb E[\|\varepsilon_m\|^2 1_{\{\widehat m=m\}}]\le\sqrt3v_m\sqrt{p_m}$. Summing gives a late selected-noise second moment at most $A_k$. By [F1], the corresponding selected bias has mean-square norm at most $b_k\sqrt{P_k}$. The mean-square triangle inequality thus bounds the late risk by $(b_k\sqrt{P_k}+\sqrt{A_k})^2$. Alternatively, $\|\varepsilon_m+f_m-x\|^2\le2\|\varepsilon_m\|^2+2b_k^2$ and $p_m\le\sqrt{p_m}$ give a late risk bound $2\sqrt3\sum_{m>k}(v_m+b_k^2)\sqrt{p_m}$. Since $v_m+b_k^2\le(v_m/v_k)R_k$, dropping the minimum in $p_m$ yields exactly $B_k$. Together with step 3.1 these prove the first finite oracle inequality. If $k=M$, both late sums are empty.

Put $c_\beta=\beta^2(\sqrt{\theta_1}-1)^2>0$ and choose a fixed nonnegative integer $J$ with $\theta_1^J\ge C''/c_\beta$. For small $s$, $\theta_2^{J+1}r<1$, so the infinite candidate sequence has $\ell=j+J<M$, $v_\ell\le\theta_2^{J+1}r$, and $b_\ell^2\le C''r\le c_\beta v_\ell$. For every $\ell\le a<b$, monotone bias gives $b_{a,b}^2\le b_a^2\le c_\beta v_a$. The reverse triangle inequality for the square-summable noise coefficient vectors gives $v_{a,b}\ge(\sqrt{v_b}-\sqrt{v_a})^2\ge(\sqrt{\theta_1}-1)^2v_a$. Thus $b_{a,b}^2\le\beta^2v_{a,b}$ and $k\le\ell$. If $k<\ell$, the oracle property implies $\mathbb E\|\widehat x_k-\widehat x_\ell\|^2\le(1+\beta^2)v_{k,\ell}\le(1+\beta^2)v_\ell$. Hence $R_k\le2(1+\beta^2)v_\ell+2R_\ell\le Cr$; the case $k=\ell$ is immediate. In particular $v_k\le Cr$ and $\log(v_k/v_0)\le CL$.

Suppose $M\ge1$ and put $w=v_0M^\delta$. For $f(v)=v\min\{1,\sqrt M(v_0/v)^{1+\gamma}\}$ one has $f(v)=v$ for $v\le w$ and $f(v)=w^{1+\gamma}v^{-\gamma}$ for $v>w$. The geometric variance lower ratio gives $\sum_{v_m\le w}v_m\le\theta_1w/(\theta_1-1)$ and $\sum_{v_m>w}v_m^{-\gamma}\le w^{-\gamma}/(1-\theta_1^{-\gamma})$, by summing the backward and forward geometric series from the respective last and first indices. Thus $A_k\le\sqrt3Kw$. Also $v_m/v_k\ge\theta_1^{m-k}$ and $\sqrt{M-m+1}\le\sqrt M$ in the definition of $B_k$ prove its stated simpler bound. The inequality $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ applied to the first late alternative in step 4.1 gives the rate-oriented oracle bound. If $M=0$, the only index is zero, its risk equals $R_0$, and all late sums vanish as stipulated.

In the mild case the stated lower variance bound gives $v_k\ge cs\alpha_k^{-1-1/a}$. Combined with step 4.2 and $r\asymp st^{-1-1/a}$, this yields $\alpha_k\ge c't$. Therefore step 1.2 gives $u_k\log(v_k/v_0)\le CsL/t=o(r)$, because $Lt^{1/a}\to0$. It follows that $D_k^2\le C(v_k+u_k\log(v_k/v_0))\le Cr$ for $k\ge1$, while $D_0=0$ handles $k=0$.

In the severe case put $H=\log(1/t)\asymp L$. If $\alpha_k\ge t$, then $\alpha_k\ge t/H$ for small $s$. If $\alpha_k<t$, the lower variance bound and $S(\alpha)\asymp(\log(1/\alpha))^p$ give $cs\alpha_k^{-1}H^{p-1}\le v_k\le Cr\le Cs t^{-1}H^p$, so again $\alpha_k\ge c't/H$. Hence $u_k\log(v_k/v_0)\le CsHL/t\le CsH^2/t\le CsH^p/t\asymp Cr$, using exactly $p\ge2$. Consequently $D_k^2\le Cr$ in this case also, with $D_0=0$ as before.

By step 2.2, $W_M=O(sL^\delta)=o(r)$: when $
u>0$, $r/s$ has a strictly positive power of $1/s$ multiplied by a fixed logarithmic power; when $
u=0$ and $	au>0$, $r=L^{-2	au}$. The rate-oriented oracle bound from step 5.1, together with $R_k\le Cr$, $b_k^2\le R_k$ and the two rate estimates just proved, therefore gives the asserted uniform risk upper bound $Cr$ in each regime. Substituting the explicit expressions for $r$ from step 2.2 gives exactly the two displayed rates and their $
u=0$ specializations. The severe proof uses $\vartheta\le1/2$ at step 5.3 and asserts only the stated upper rate, preserving the given qualification and grid hypotheses. This completes both the finite oracle and rate conclusions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: Put $Q_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j\xi_j^2$, $v_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j$, and $w_n=\sum_{j\le n}a_j^2$. On finite intervals integration by parts with $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$ gives $\int x^{2k}\phi(x)\,dx=[-x^{2k-1}\phi(x)]+(2k-1)\int x^{2k-2}\phi(x)\,dx$. The boundary terms vanish at infinity; the integrals converge since a polynomial times $e^{-x^2/2}$ is bounded by a constant times $e^{-x^2/4}$, whose integral is finite by [F3] and the given unit Gaussian integral. Starting from $\int\phi=1$ therefore gives $\mathbb E\xi_j^2=1$ and $\mathbb E\xi_j^4=3$. Thus $\mathbb E Q_n=v_n$ and finite independence gives $\mathbb E Q_n^2=v_n^2+2w_n$. Also $u\le v$ and $w\le uv\le v^2$.

The measurable series $Q_n\uparrow Q$ satisfies $\mathbb E Q=v$ by [F1]; hence $Q<\infty$ almost surely, since [F2] gives $\mathbb P(Q\ge r)\le v/r$ for every $r>0$. Extending $N$ by zero on the null exceptional set does not change an integral. Applying [F1] also to $Q_n^2\uparrow Q^2$ proves $\mathbb E N^4=v^2+2w\le3v^2$.

Suppose $u>0$. For $0<s<(2u)^{-1}$ the scalar substitution $y=\sqrt{1-2sa_j}\,x$ in [F3], using the supplied unit density, gives $\mathbb E e^{s a_j\xi_j^2}=(1-2sa_j)^{-1/2}$. Finite factorization [F4] and the power-series inequality $-\log(1-z)-z\le z^2/[2(1-z)]$ for $0\le z<1$ therefore give $$\log\mathbb E e^{s(Q_n-v_n)}=\sum_{j\le n}\left[-sa_j-\tfrac12\log(1-2sa_j)\right]\le\frac{s^2w_n}{1-2us}.$$ If $w_n>0$, apply [F2] to this exponential and choose $s=\sqrt t/(\sqrt{w_n}+2u\sqrt t)$. Substitution gives $-s(2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut)+s^2w_n/(1-2us)=-t$, so $\mathbb P\{Q_n>v_n+2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut\}\le e^{-t}$. If $w_n=0$, then $Q_n=v_n=0$ almost surely and this inequality is immediate.

The deterministic levels $v_n+2\sqrt{w_nt}+2ut$ converge to $v+2\sqrt{wt}+2ut$. Whenever $Q$ strictly exceeds this final level, sufficiently large $n$ have $Q_n$ exceeding their corresponding levels. The probability of this eventual-event set is at most the lower limit of their probabilities, as follows directly by countable additivity applied to unions of intersections. Step 2.2 thus gives the first tail inequality. Since $w\le uv$ and $v+2\sqrt{uvt}+2ut\le(\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut})^2$, the second follows. If $u=0$, all weights vanish and both bounds hold directly.

The second tail bound makes the set defining $q(t)$ nonempty and implies $0\le q(t)\le\sqrt v+\sqrt{2ut}$. This set is upward closed. Every $q(t)+1/n$ therefore belongs to it: by the definition of an infimum some member lies strictly below that number. The events $\{N>q(t)+1/n\}$ increase to $\{N>q(t)\}$, so countable additivity gives $\mathbb P(N>q(t))\le e^{-t}$. When $v=0$, step 2.1 gives $N=0$ almost surely and the quantile is zero. Finally, in a fixed orthonormal system the squared norm of the finite Gaussian sum is $Q_n$; finiteness of $Q$ gives norm convergence of that series and the asserted norm interpretation.
